Mr. Speaker, on Thursday last I entered my protest against this procedure. The First Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) agreed with me that I was right, because he asked the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Cowan) to withdraw the motion he had made. I think that the conclusion come to then was that it was quite time enough to ask that the committees should have leave to sit during the sessions of the House when the committees made representation that they required such permission. There has been no meeting of tbe Railway Committee since then, and consequently no resolution passed asking permission to sit during the sittings of the House. The hon. member for Victoria, Nova Scotia (Mr. Wm. Ross) made the suggestion that the committees meet at nine o'clock. I assented to that. I am quite willing that that suggestion should be acted upon. But I do protest against standing committees meeting while the business of the House 'is in progress. We want to be here while the House is conducting its business ; and, since the government has thought fit to commence the morning sittings-to-morrow morning they begin, I believe-some provision should be made by which members can attend to their duties. I, for one, do not propose to absent myself from tbe House in order to attend the meetings of the Railway Committee, nor shall I willingly absent myself from the work of the Railway Committee. There are other important committees besides tbe Railway Committee, and, if you insist on these committees meeting while the House is in session, no doubt the .government will expect to get their estimates through in our absence in a very short time. This motion is contrary to precedent-at any rate, it is contrary to common sense. The hon. minister (Mr. Hyman), I trust, will pardon me if I say that his motion is not in accordance with common sense. It is not reasonable to suppose that we can be in two places at tbe same time, or that we are to desert our duties here in order to attend to the duties of the Railway Committee, particularly when the difficulty may be overcome by having the committee meet at nine o'clock, and sit until eleven if necessary. I must again enter my solemn protest against this proceeding.

Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding that the Railway Committee-as, I think, all will agree-have laboured very assiduously during the session, there still remain some important matters to be dealt witli by that committee. It is true that this motion is not recommended by tbe

committee, but, as the committee has been called to meet to-morrow at eleven o'clock, I took it upon myself to bring in this motion. Why not have the committee meet at nine o'clock ?

Unfortunately, the committee has already been called for eleven o'clock, and announcements to that effect have been made. Well, the whole difficulty can be got over in this way, Mr. Speaker-when the House meets to-morrow you can simply call it one o'clock, and leave the chair.

Bill is to correct two or three errors which, through inadvertence or oversight, crept into the Representation Act of last session. Sections 7 and 8 of the Representation Act slipped into their present position in the body of the Act through error. They are taken from the Quebec Act, Revised Statutes of Quebec, chapter 2, sections 67 and 68, which defines the provincial electoral districts. The intention was to insert these particular sections 6 and 7 where they ought to be, in the Quebec schedule. They have been incorporated in the body of the Act, which would make them applicable to the whole Dominion. Of course this is absolutely impossible under the system of dividing constituencies, as they exist elsewhere.
There are other changes that refer to Ontario. When the Bill of last session was prepared, an Ontario Act of 1901 was overlooked. This is one of the Acts which are passed yearly by the legislature of that province, entitled ' Acts to amend the Statute Law. This necessitates a change in the description of the electoral districts of Thunder Bay and Rainy River, and the two ridings of Algoma. Not at all. These figures arose by reason of the representations which were made to the department and to the minister then in charge that the enginemen, conductors and trainmen on other railways in Canada were receiving

larger compensation than the government railway was paying and the principle was recognized, measurably at least, if not to its full extent, that the government railway should pay as high a standard of wages as is paid by other corporations throughout Canada. Recently, when the Telegrahers Union were heard by myself, it was shown conclusively, especially in respect to the Canadian Pacific Railway on their eastern division, that they were paying a larger wage and larger salaries than were being paid by the Intercolonial Railway. I ventured to recognize the justice of the claim and there has been and will be found to be an increase in the expenditure of the department because of the action taken by myself at the time they were here. The same is true in respect to the section men, the conductors, the brakemen, the locomotive drivers and firemen, and in fact in all branches of the service. In the stores department, even, among the freight checkers, and the freight handlers at all points along the Intercolonial Railway there have been large increases. In some instances the increases have ranged from twenty to twenty-five, and even there have been increases within the last two or three years of fifty-per cent in the wages paid to the employees of the Intercolonial Railway for the purpose of recognizing the right of these men to be paid a wage equal to the amount paid for like services by other roads. In addition to that the industrial life of the country is such that men can receive from private corporations larger wages than have been paid by the Intercolonial Railway. Take it down in the maritime provinces, at Moncton, at Amherst, anywhere along the line .where there is great activity in the industrial life of the country, private corporations, foundries, machine shops, in fact in all branches of industrial life, they are paying a larger wage than that which was being paid to the men by the Intercolonial Railway. Therefore, it was found necessary, just and equitable, that there should be this increase. By reason of such an increase, by reason of the recognition of the claims of labour, I am forced to-day as representing the Railway Department to acknowledge before parliament and to present to the country a financial condition that is not as we would like it to be.

I have not that with me. Now, the figures which I have presented to-day, particularly as respects the current year ending 30th of June last, rather cause one to reflect as to the conditions surrounding the Intercolonial Railway. In presenting the figures, I have no apology to make. I bear in mind this fact- that the Intercolonial was built, not as a commercial railroad, but as a railroad necessary in the interest of the Dominion with a view to cementing the separated provinces. I recognize the fact that the business element did not enter very largely into consideration in the choice of routes. I recognize, more than that, that there was, at the inception of this Dominion, a condition of things that led the framers of confederation to take all these elements into consideration. And, finally I recognize that these conditions have not very materially changed. The long route was chosen. That portion of the Intercolonial which, speaking generally, may be described as the line to connect the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is to-day a paving portion of the line. The portion which has not paid is that long route around the northern section of New Brunswick to the St. Lawrence river, and so along its [shore. Now, what were the conditions which prevailed at that time ? The people of the maritime provinces had free use of a very cheap means of transportation from the markets of the world to practically every community throughout those provinces-they had the Atlantic sea-board. Their importations were very largely by water. The whole southern coast of Nova Scotia was within a stone's throw of Boston. The Chignecto bay and Minas basin sections of the Bay of Fundy were in close touch with the American sea-board and carried on

their commerce of export and import day by day throughout the whole season-not merely during the time of summer navigation but throughout the winter months as well. That was not, it will be acknowledged, in the interest of the Dominion, it was not in harmony with the idea of a confederation of the provinces. It was necessary that some attempt should be made to bring" about an interchange of products between the people of Quebec and Ontario and the people of the maritime provinces. A great many people say that the route was chosen and the road was built for the benefit of the people of the maritime provinces. I take issue at once upon any such statement. It was specially in the interest of Ontario, of the wheat-growing sections, the flour producing sections of our Dominion that there should be rail transportation between those sections and the maritime provinces. And, in order that that rail transportation might be practically effective, it was necessary to establish rates which would enable interchange to take place.
The Intercolonial must be recognized as bound on two sides by great waterways. During the summer months it must compete w'it'h the navigation in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and in addition in the Straits of Northumberland, where sea-going vessels can reach every section of the north shores of New Brunswick, every section of Prince Edward Island and: of Cape Breton, and many sections of Nova Scotia; while on the other hand the Intercolonial must compete with the water-ways of the Atlantic sea-board, it must compete with the Portland traffic from Ontario by rail, if necessary. or with the traffic to Boston, and thence by water to different sections of the maritime provinces. Necessarily the rates had to be low, they had to be trimmed with a view to meeting this very serious competition. We are told to-day that the lakes are competing with railway transportation. If there is any force in that argument with respect to inland trade, there is ten-fold force in it with respect to the competition with which the Intercolonial is met by the Atlantic sea-going vessels during all seasons of the year, and during the summer months by navigation on the St. Lawrence. Now those conditions prevailed, and it was necessary to establish freight rates which. I grant you, might from one standpoint be considered as conventional, but which are a necessity if you are to cement these provinces together and bring about the interchange of trade which is so necessary for the well-being of the Dominion. To-day we are suffering in a measure because of that. While it is true that the traffic on the Intercolonial has grown, while it is true that trade has grown, there has not been one per cent of an increase in the rates during all that period; and the people of the east parti-

eularly, and the people of the west as well, the merchants of Montreal, of Toronto, of Hamilton, of Guelph, of all the manufacturing centres of Ontario and Quebec, t'he very moment there was the slightest intimation of an increase in the freight rates along the line of the Intercolonial, would enter a protest, and the government, I care not what government might be In power and administering the affairs of the Intercolonial, would be powerless to make such increases along the line of the Intercolonial. I do not believe it would' be 'in the interest of tike trade of the Dominion to do so. 1 believe that the Intercolonial is destined i be one of the greatest and most valuable assets of the Dominion. Although you cannot measure its benefits by dollars and cents, I believe that in the past it has been one of the best assets of the Dominion of Canada in cementing the provinces together, in making t'he people of the various provinces acquainted with each other ; and in that way it has been rendering a service to the Dominion which no other agency could perform.
Now, Sir, the problem which confronts the Department of Railways at this moment, and which confronts me as responsible for t'he administration of the government system of railways, is this : We have recognized the requirements of labour, we have recognized that because of the conditions which prevail in all sections covered by the Intercolonial, it is necessary to pay the employees of that road a better wage than has hitherto been paid. We have recognized that in all departments. W e shall be obliged further to recognize that because of the industrial growth of the country, because of the conditions which prevail to-day. Everywhere there is activity. The employees in the industrial establishments along the line of the Intercolonial are receiving a much higher rate of wage than they were receiving a few years ago. Today the Canadian Pacific Railway is paying a higher rate of wage to its employees, and I am sure I am wit'hin the judgment of this House when I say that the government of Canada cannot afford to pay a less rate of wage to its employees than does the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. True, you may say that the Canadian Pacific Railway is a dividend paying corporation, that large sums are being distributed year by year among its shareholders. Still I say that although the Intercolonial cannot show as favourable a balance sheet, although it cannot make the same distribution of its earnings, yet in many other ways it is making a return to tne people of the Dominion, not merely to the people of Quebec and the maritime provinces, but to those of Ontario and the west, which cannot be measured in dollars and cents but which has a value above all pecuniary considerations. Therefore we must recognize that we cannot enjoy tthis advantage without paying a fair and just equivalent to the men who are engaged in the management and operation of that railway. This will be admitted, I am sure. Moreover, we must recognize that these wages are a fixed charge upon the Intercolonial. You caunot reduce them. Nor are you in the same position as a private corporation, who, when they increase the wages, can at the same time increase the rates. Not many weeks ago we saw in the newspapers a statement to t'he effect that some railway corporations that were obliged to pay higher wages to their employees were at the same time turning the screws upon their patrons and charging them a higher freight rate. The ,Intercolonial cannot do that. If it 'is not found in written words in the compact of confederation, there is a conventional understanding recognized by all, t'hat the rates on the Intercolonial shall not be increased, and that the people shall enjoy the benefits of that road at the lowest rates compatible with its maintenance. These benefits me equally accessible to the manufacturing industries of western Canada and to the merchants and distributors. The good resulting is not confined to any one section of Canada. Therefore it is a problem to which, while I have the honour to hold the position I now occupy, I must address my every energy, I shall act with zeal and activity to see if something cannot be done whereby the financial conditions of the Intercolonial can be improved. I believe that can be done in a measurable degree by the modernization of the road. It is true, we have started out to remedy many defects with respect to curves and gradients. I believe that work should continue. We are endeavouring to secure the very best and most modern equipment, improvements in the class of locomotives, in the class of cars, making stronger bridges, and other betterments to harmonize therewith. You cannot have heavy engines without having heavier bridges, you cannot have large trains passing over the road without removing the defects in its curves and In its gradients. Modernize the road and I feel assured that you can minimize the expense in carrying the traffic over it. The question of passenger traffic, as far as it relates to the whole line, must be recognized in this light, that we carry passengers from Montreal to St. John for the same rate as is paid to the Canadian Pacific Railway, and yet there is a very great discrimination against us in the matter of distance. The same is true in respect to the carrying of our freight. We can only charge the same rates as are charged by the Canadian Pacific Railway and yet we have the longer haul. We have additional employees to be paid. We cannot certainly do it at the same rate. Our expenses upon the whole

must be necessarily larger. We have a longer mileage and yet we are paid according to the minimum mileage. Under these circumstances I am sure this House and the country must recognize the difficulties in the way of making the Intercolonial Railway the success that we all hope and desire it may be. I shall have to address myself to the solution of these problems. I do not know how successful I may be, but in so far as the modernizing of the road is concerned, if that can be accomplished and if parliament will aid in the accomplishment of that by generous and substantial votes, we will have accomplished some good in that direction and in the maintenance of the road. I do not pledge myself that we shall skimp the employees, that we shall starve them or that the pay that is given to them shall in any way show a shrinkage because of the conditions with which we have to deal. The men of the Intercolonial Railway must be paid equal to met anywhere in Canada. That is their due, it is their right, and I do not think that there is any spirit in this parliament or out of it anywhere in Canada which would favour a proposal that these men shall be underpaid or paid less than is paid by private corporations in employment of a like character. There is, I think, reason for very great hope in the matter of the traffic in the eastern section of our Dominion and along the line of the Intercolonial Railway. It is true that in respect to the Sydney trade we are obliged to give very reasonable rates in competition with the water rates. It is true that in bringing our coal from the Nova Scotia collieries to Montreal-and we can get very little above that city-we ai'e obliged to give the very lowest possible rates in competition with the water rates. It is true we cannot load these coal cars oil their return with the ordinary merchandise that goes from the western section of the country to the eastern districts. It is true that all these are disadvantages under which we labour . but there is growing up along the line of the Intercolonial Railway in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia industries which will contribute year after year, which are contributing to-day, which have contributed the last year very materially to the freight traffic of the Intercolonial Railway. I have endeavoured to deal with the financial conditions in a frank and candid manner. I do not wish to withhold one single feature from this House or from the country in respect to the management of the road. I believe that the road, although it shows a deficit, more than makes up its equivalent in another way, and I believe that the Intercolonial Railway should be and will be sustained and maintained by the people of Canada.

The minister evidently does not understand what the prerequisite is for granting a salary. First of all you form the skeleton of the sum that is required for the purpose of administering the department. You pay every man in it according to his supposed departmental value. Then you apply to Council and you state the number of clerks you require for the purpose of carrying on your business. You state the value of the particular service that each man is expected to perform, not the value of the man, but the value of the service jthat he performs. You fix the salary of each official. Then the law provides that when the deputy minister, with the concurrence of the minister, recommends the statutory increase, it has to be approved by Council, and after that you I>ut the amount in the estimates. But it is not the value of the man you consider, it is the value of the service he renders to the country. You make an estimate of so many clerks at $1,500, so many at $1,200, so many at $1,000, add so on. It is a curious anomaly to say :	We have so many deserving
clerks. Here is a man who fills a particular office. Suppose you want a superior officer, the service he performs to the country is only worth $1,500 a year, though the man may be worth $10,000. Then according to the value of the man you increase his salary. The salaries are fixed for your departmental staff, and then the Civil Service law gives them an increase per annum. When vacancies occur by death, or absence, or superannuation, you fill them up ; but the amount that is paid ought to be always the same unless the duties of the office are increased, or unless you require a larger staff to carry on the business. In that case the additions have to be approved by Council and reasons assigned before the vote is put in the estimates. In this case the minister must remember that it is not simply a question of paying a man $100 a year additional, what we are discussing is the principle. If the minister had been in the House as long as I have been, and a member of a government as well as a member of the opposition, he would have heard the tirades that used to be made week after week and year after year on a single item occurring in the estimates asking for a grant to an officer notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act. Mr. McMullen, formerly a member of this House and now a distinguished senator, used to enlarge for hours upon the enormity of paying sums notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act. What is the use of having such an Act, he used to say, what is the use of having a law on the statute-book if it is being constantly evaded ? That is the reason we are questioning this vote. I would not have any objection to it in itself. This man may be an appointment of mine, he may be a deserving officer, a man too big for the position at $1,400 a year. It may be a shame to employ a man of his ability to perform work that is only worth to the country $1,400 a year. But that is no reason why he should get anything iu excess of what he is entitled to under the law. It is the principle that we object to, we object to this constant enlargement of the expenditure in the various departments. You form a department here, for instance, the Department of Trade and Commerce, which is only to cost a few thousand a year, and then to give importance to the minister, the staff increases from year to year until each minister is jealous of the other if there is a larger expenditure in one department than the other. What is the effect ? The country is burdened with a lot of officials who are not perhaps required for the proper discharge of their duties and to which enormous salaries are being paid.

If this gentleman continued in the same office and gave the same return to the country for two years longer he would be entitled under the 'law to $1,700. I recognize the value of the work he is doing. I recognize the recommendation made by the deputy in that regard and I say that justice should be done now to this gentleman and not wait for two years. When this recommendation was made, I concurred in it. It was done at a time when I did not know the official and had not seen him. But the facts were given to me by the deputy.
Hon. WILLIAM ROSiS. There is not a minister, however brilliant, who has not to rely upon his deputy for information of this kind Here is a deputy who has grown gray I was almost going to say grown bald, in the service of this country, and who! states that this man is entitled to receive this increase, and the minister relies on that information. That is all that any minister can do, because it is impossible for ministers to have information as to the merits or demerits of all the clerks under them.

Has Mr. Ross any greater responsibility now than he had a year
ago ?

I cannot say that he has, and I add that two years hence he will

not probably have any greater responsibility but will be entitled to the $1,700.

I have no objection to Mr. Ross getting the $1,700, I am satisfied that if he were not worth it, the deputy would net recommend it. But I will remind the minister that last year, when the government were amending the Civil Service Act, if they had accepted the proposition I made that all first-class clf/'ks should be given a yearly increase of $100, Mr. Ross would have had the $1,700 this year without any trouble, and without being under any compliment. Is it the intention of the minister, in the case of officials who have not received their statutory increases, to make them up to them ?
I do not know whether there are any who have not had their statutory increases. If there are any they have not been brought to my notice.
But if there are any 1
I will certainly give them the same consideration that I am giving to Mr. Ross.
Will the minister also state where he got the authority to give the Statutory increase of last year ? I cannot find it in his estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think perhaps I can explain that. Last year, it will be remembered, after the estimates were dealt with, the Civil Service Act was amended, and provision was made by a general vote that increases might be paid to any clerks entitled to receive them. I think it is likely that this gentleman came under the terms of that general clause, which would explain why the item did not appear in the estimates.;

I think we are entitled to have that explanation clearly from the minister in charge of the department. The Minister of Finance does not tell us as a fact that this is so ; he says he supposes that it is so.

My deputy informs me that these three first-class clerks for whom it was proposed to have an appropriation of $1,900 each this year, received $1,850 during the fiscal year 1903-4. That was paid, and it was paid necessarily with the concurrence of the Auditor General. It is proposed in the item under discussion to give the statutory increases to all these different clerks, with the exception of Mr. Ross, and his case I think I have very fuliy explained to the committee.

I understand that several organizations of workingmen in the employ of the Intercolonial Railway have made application to the minister for further increases in the wages paid to them. Might Mr. EMMERSON.
I ask whether the hon. gentleman has reached any conclusion ?
I have stated in my general statement that other increases would be necessary in connection with the emJ ployees of the Intercolonial.
Is the hon. gentleman going to consider favourably the application made ?
I am under arrangements to meet the men at Moncton immediately at the close of the session, and go over the whole schedule.
Will provision be made in the supplementary estimates for increased remuneration ?
That is contained in the general vote for the Intercolonial.
And that is being taken ?
That is being provided for.

I see that the Minister of Finance is right and the Minister of Railways wrong, in stating that there was a supplementary vote. It says at the end of the Civil Service Act:
And during the financial year ending on the 30th day of June, 1904, there may be paid from and out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada such sums of money as may not have been voted by parliament but are required for payment of such salaries and increases of salaries as are authorized by this Act.
If we had obtained that information some time ago we would have made better progress.

In reference to the item for a law clerk, the minister has explained that the reason for the reduction of the salary from $2,100 to $1,925 is that the gentleman who formerly occupied this position has left the service and a. new man has come in. Is he an entirely new man ?
He was promoted. He had been the assistant law clerk and was promoted to the position of law clerk.
Is he a barrister ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, he is a barrister.
How long had he been in the service and what salary had he received previously ?
He has been in the service about three years. He began as assistant law clerk with a salary of $1,200, but this was subsequently increased to $1,400.

Then we are to understand that a clerk who has been in the service for three years arrived at a salary of $1,200 and was subsequently increased to

$1,400. What is the initial salary in this office ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think that $1,900 was the original salary for the position of law clerk. The last occupant of the position was getting $2,100 or $2,200. Mr. Hansard's salary was increased while he was assistant law clerk and when his superior officer retired he was promoted to the position of law clerk at a salary, I think, of $1,900.
Mr. Hansard last year received $1,500.

I am not in favour of 'cutting salaries too low, particularly, as some one suggests, in the case of a lawyer, but what I point out is that I understood the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) to so say some little time ago that $1,400 was the initial salary for this service. In that case I think it is unreasonable to start this gentleman at $1,925 ; if his predecessor was receiving $2,100, the difference of $175 seems to be very slight. I am not in a position to say it is wrong, but I call the attention of the minister to it.

I want to know if the minister has received any communications from the maintenance of -way employees on other roads, that is the Brotherhood of Maintenance of Way Men, in regard to the rates paid to that class of men on the Intercolonial Railway. I understand that the rate paid on the Intercolonial Railway is less than that paid oh the other roads. I want to know if the minister has received any resolutions or applications for an increase so as to bring the rate of wages up to that paid to the same class of employees on other roads. This is a very important class of work and I think these men are possibly *quite as much entitled to an increase as some of those whom the hon. minister is looking after at the present time.

The information received by my hon. friend is certainly very inaccurate. The facts are exactly the reverse. The Intercolonial Railway is paying more to trackmen 'than any other road in eastern Canada-I do not speak of the west, because there is a higher standard there ; a dollar means more in the east than in the west. I have received no communications from any organization but if I did receive any they could only represent what is the fact ; that the petitioners were not receiving as much pay as those on the Intercolonial Railway doing similar service.

I wish to read some resolutions that have been sent to me in regard to the matter, so that the minister will be able to see the reason I have in bringing the matter to his attention :
To the government of the Dominion of Canada.
The following resolution was put and carried unanimously :-
That we, the members of subordinate Lodge No. 145 of the International Brotherhood of Maintenance of Way employees (employees on the central division of the Canadian Pacific Railway), do heartily favour an increase of wages to all the maintenance of way employees on our government railways so that the purchasing power of their wages will be equal to what it was a few years ago.
And that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to our Dominion government through our representative, Mr. N. Bbyd, M.P.
When is that dated.
One of these resolutions is dated September 21, 1903.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This subject has been dealt with, I think, about that time.

I have another one here which I shall also read, so that it may be on record for the minister to see.
Moved by Brother Woolsey, seconded by Brother J. Wilson, that we, the members of Minnedosa Division No. 163 of Maintenance of Way Employees of America, assembled, do by unanimous vote desire to place on record that we strongly disapprove of the low scale of wages paid hy the government roads of Canada to the maintenance of way employees, such wages being below the wages paid hy other Canadian roads for same class of labour, and we wish as voters to enlist your aid both in the House and out of it towards rectifying this injustice.
I have a letter very strongly urging me to bring this matter to the attention of the government, and, if necessary to urge it in the House. If the matter has been attended to, it will remove the necessity for my doing so. But I would ask the minister to tell me what the wages are, so that I may make a comparison.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The Minister of Railways has stated that he did not receive these communications. But I may explain that while I- was acting minister of that department, I received probably these very communications, certainly some communication of the same tenor. This was some months ago. The matter was then under consideration. In fact, it had been referred to in the discussions of last session and intimation had been given that it would be inquired into at the close of the session. It was inquired into and the wages of the maintenance of way employees, trackmen as they are usually called, were increased.
What was the increase ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The ordinary trackmen were receiving $1.30, and this was increased to $1.40. and the section foremen received a corresponding increase. I think this is above the wages paid by any of the great railways of Canada. In case of other branches of the railway service I was willing to take the expenditure of other railways where the men were getting paid at a more advanced * figure than those on the government road.

But, I thought that in the ease of the trackmen who were lowest in the scale of pay in the service, we need not take the scale of the other railways, but that $1.30, the amount we were then giving, was rather low, and, irrespective of what other railways paid we should advance it to $1.40. That was done some months ago. And, as I am reminded by an hon. friend, in some sections, I believe the amount was made $1.50, a distinction being made with regard to the various grades of stations, so that, .under certain conditions, there was an increase to $1.50.
Civil Government-Department of Railways and Canals-contingencies :-
Printing and stationery	$5,000
Contingencies	 3,000
We should have some explanation of this.
This is the same vote as last year-the usual vote.

That is not sufficient. Is all last year's vote expended ? In these cases. I think we had better go back to the practice of some years ago and get an explanation from the minister of what the money is for. It can hardly be taken for granted that because $S,000 was required last year therefore $8,000 will be required this year.

This is the usual vote. For the year ending 30th June 1903, the amount spent on printing and stationery was $0,061.98 and on contingencies $2,439.37. So, the amount of the vote was exceeded and I think that a supplementary vote has been asked for to meet the expenditure.

This shows the utility of asking for information. It is very clear and very satisfactory. We have, had $6,000 odd spent on printing and stationery-no separation made between the items of printing and stationery-and $2,000 odd for something else making a total of $8,000. Now, what could be more satisfactory 7 And, if we had not asked we would not have received this information.

What proportion of this printing is done outside of the Printing Bureau ? . I see that last year a considerable amount was done for the department by newspaper offices in different parts of the country.
This is all done in the Printing Bureau.
Was the report of the department this year done in the Printing Bureau ?
Yes, so I am informed.

This vote, I take it, applies to the office here. But the printing on the Mr. FIELDING. '
Intercolonial such as folders and all the other printing
That is not in this vote.
But is the minister able to say what proportion of the general printing required for the Intercolonial is done outside the Printing Bureau ?
The folders, &c\, have to be done in offices that are in touch with the central offices at Moncton.

Would it not be possible for the printing, of which, as I see by the Auditor General's Report, there is a large amount, to be done in the Printing Bureau ? Why is not the printing done here ? I see that it is spread over most of the newspaper organs of the hon. gentlemen opposite in the maritime provinces, sometimes under contract and sometimes without any contract. In consequence of this, a difficulty arose last year between the Auditor General and the employees of my hon. friend's (Mr. Emmer-son's) department.

I do not think it would be possible to have this printing done here. But I shall be prepared to discuss that question under the proper item. I do not think the subject properly arises under this item.

It seems to me that discussion might properly arise under this item as this relates to printing for the department. However, my hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) may desire to get information on the subject.. I will raise the question again on another item. There is another point I wish to speak about, though it does not exactly concern printing. The minister will remember that we had some correspondence in regard to the abandonment to the town of Lachine of the use of the old canal bank there. The bank is not now used by the government. As I explained in the correspondence that I had with the minister on behalf of the municipality, this canal bank has become an eyesore, and. now that the summer holidays are beginning, the authorities of Lachine are extremely anxious to obtain the use-during pleasure, of course -of that canal bank, in order to give it a more creditable appearance. I made a similar application a few years, ago, but, at that time there was an obstacle in the way in the shape of a projected railway to pass through. That obstacle has been removed, and, as the minister knows, there is no reason at all why the authorities of Lachine should not have a favourable answer to their repeated representations. I merely wish to inquire, as we are now getting into July, whether it would not be possible to grant their request.

That lease could only be entered into by an Order in Council ap-

proved by His Excellency. The matter is now under consideration, and I hope it will be concluded before long. Besides, that matter does not come under the present vote.

I know that. But in a matter of this kind I do not think we are obliged, in discussing the estimates, to confine ourselves absolutely to the item under discussion. I think we have a right to urge any grievance we have, or any complaint, before we vote the amount. I have not bothered my hon. friend unduly with regard to that question. It seems to me such a simple question that there must be some extraordinary reason for not concluding it when the town at present is so urgent. When the matter was taken up three or four years ago there was some objection, I think" there was a line of railway projected through there, but that objection has been removed. From the correspondence I had with my hon. friend I understood that it was merely a matter of routine, of getting the Order in Council through, and giving the town of Lachine the intimation and passing that lease, as my hon. friend stated a moment ago. I would like to know if there is any cause for this delay, beyond the ush'al icause that a certain time is required to pass it through Council, because the town of Lachine desires to improve, embellish and arrange that whole canal bank before tbe summer is finished.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think we had better not pursue this discussion further, as it is outside the item before the committee.
I would like to have your ruling on that point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: My ruling is this, that when a resolution is before the committee, the committee can, if they choose, discuss the whole resolution in a general way, but when they have taken up a particular item, relevancy is one of the rules that govern the discussion, and when the item is passed it cannot be referred to any more. We cannot discuss any question outside the proposition, before the committee unless the committee is willing to allow an irrelevant discussion to go on.
If you rule that, upon an item in the minister's department, I am not entitled to ascertain the cause of the delay in this instance, I shall have to bow to your ruling.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There will probably be some other item under which the hon. gentleman can bring this subject up.
I merely wanted to know on behalf of my constituency if this matter will he concluded before it is too late.

We have had some correspondence ou the matter, it is now
being considered in the department, and I. think we will reach finality with respect to.
It within a very short time. I am endeavouring to dispose of it as speedily as possible. There has been a great deal of work in the department in its relation to the-executive council, but as soon as this matter can be disposed of, I "will answer my hon.. friend, and I hope it will be very soon.

I see there is an item here for contingencies, although the amount is very small, and I would like to take oc-cassion to call the attention of the minister to the condition of the bridges across the Rideau icanal between upper and lower town. The Sappers' bridge particularly is in a deplorable condition.
They are in the Public Works Department.

But these bridges cross tlie Rideau canal, and the hon. gentleman's department lias charge of canals. It is possible that the Improvement Commissioners have them In charge. But they are government property, and I thought well to bring tbe matter before the attention of the government. The bridges are certainly in a deplorable condition, they are not safe so far as the- sidewalks are concerned.
I am informed that these bridges are under the charge of the Public Works Department.

The Sappers' bridge used to be under tbe control of tlie Rideau canal, it was built by the Rideau canal authorities, and was under their control. It may have passed over to the Public Works Department-, but I do not know how.

Then there is an extra amount which will be required for moving certain buildings. grading the station grounds, rearranging the tracks and for certain land and legal expenses in connection therewith totalling $14,000. This makes $86,000 which we will require for the purpose of increasing the accommodation at Sydney.

The total expenditure for improved and increased accommodation at Sydney beginning with 1896 down to June 30. 1903, is $387,771.73. Then the ex-nenditure from June 30, 1903, to May 1, 1904, was $11,107.37, making a total of $398,879.10, so that the total estimated cost of improved

and increased accommodation at Sydney Will be $498,771.73.
That will leave $100,000 yet to be expended ?
Yes.
What is the reason that so very little of the money appropriated last year was spent ?

It was so late in the season it was found inexpedient to have the work carried on. The work involves the construction of a new station and general improvements around and about it and the work could not be carried on at that time of the year.

Perhaps the bon. minister will be able to give the expenditure on capital account for last year. In this whole item of the Intercolonial Railway there is a revote of $036,485, appropriations not required for 1894-5 amounting to $2,034,084.84 and a total appropriation of $3,717,284.84. Deducting $2,034,084.84 the total amount chargeable to capital account with Intercolonial Railway alone was over a million dollars. Is that not so ?
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to ask what the total expenditure on the capital account of the Intercolonial Railway was up to the end of last year ?
Up to the end of 1903-4. You say that you only- have the returns up to the 31st May.

I have not the total expenditure but I have promised to furnish it. I could not very well get it this evening as the clerks were not in the office but I will give the hon. gentleman the total expenditure up to June 30, 1903, chargeable to oapital account.
We have that but we want the expenditure for 1903-4, the amount voted last year.
That is for the current year ending the 30th June, 1904 ?
Yes.
I will furnish that information to-morrow.

But the hon. gentleman has given us one item of expenditure up to the 31st May, the expenditure at Sydney. The( total amount of the revote is $636,485 and the appropriations not required for 1904-5, $2,034,084.84. Deduct this amount from the appropriations for 1903-4 and it leaves over $1,000,000 chargeable to capital account alone, that the Intercolonial Railway have expended up to 31st May or up to the 1st July. That is correct, is it not ?
If I follow the hon. gentleman I think that would be it. I can give him the total up to the end of April of the actual expenditure on capital account. It it $1,362,070.38.
On capital account for ten months ?
On capital account for ten months.

On the Intercolonial
Railway ?
On the Intercolonial Railway.
Well, then you have nothing to expend for May and June. You see that there is an amount at your disposal of about a million dollars.
This $1,046,000 you have expended in ten months and you must have something to expend in the next two months.
The total amount appropriated on capital account to the Intercolonial Railway for 1903-4 was $3,717,284.84.
That is right.
We have expended up to the end of April of that sum $1,362,070.38.
But does not the hon. minister see this ? You ask for a revote of $663,4S5. You say that you do not require of last year's appropriations, $2,034,084.84.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That does not apply to the past year. That does not mean that that amount is not required for the year for which it is voted. It means that similar works are not required for the coming year. The amount is not required for 1904-5.
It is not required for 1904-5 but it is not expended under the vote of 1903-4.
This is the part of the vote that is not required.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: These words do not put any limitation on the expenditures of the past year. They only make a comparison between the two years. There are various sums which were not required to be repeated and which total up to the amount stated, but these words do not put any limitation on the minister's expenditure for the past year.
You took a vote for 1903-4 on capital account of $3,717,284.84 for railways and canals. You state that of that $3,717,284.84 you do not require $2,034,-084.S4.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, we do not say anything of the kind.

591&
It says :	' appropriations not required for 1904-5.'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Exactly ; similar votes are not required for the coming year.

Any way the minister will give me at the next meeting of the committee the expenditure to the 31st of May, and the estimated expenditure on capital account for the next month hoth on the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island railways and all the other works that will be under discussion.

Has the minister had his attention directed to a resolution passed by the Sydney Board of Trade and endorsed by the Halifax Board of Trade, with respect to a night train between Halifax, Sydney and North Sydney ? The resolution cl' the" Halifax Board of Trade passed last March, is as follows
That the Halifax Board of Trade approves the resolution of the Sydney Board of Trade regarding the immediate need of a night train between Halifax, Sydney and North Sydney, and that it urges the Intercolonial Railway authorities to grant the demand for the same as soon as they are able to do so.
Has this matter been under consideration and if so with what result?

I received a copy of this resolution from the Halifax and Sydney Board of Trade. The question has been very carefully considered both by the Intercolonial Railway management and myself. There are now two daily trains from Sydney ; one in the early morning and the other at mid-day, and these trains are found very convenient for the people on the intermediate stations all along the line. There are many good reasons why we should have a night train ; it would convenience a limited few so far as I could judge from the facts, but the present traffic would not justify three trains daily, and taking into consideration the convenience to the greatest number it was thought that 'it would not he advisable to substitute a night train for one of the day trains.

I entirely endorse the decision of the department in this matter. It would be very inconvenient for tlie travelling public generally if one of these day trains was taken off and run at night. I would remind the minister that there is1 a fast freight running between Halifax and Sydney, and probably wifhout any great additional expense, a sleeping car could be attached to that train. This, for some time at least would meet the requirements of night travel.
Does the freight train leave at night ?
No; the hour would have to be changed.

One difficulty in running a night train is the additional expense of crossing the Straits. We hope the traffic will grow sa that it will justify the putting on of a night train, but at present that is not the case.
Intercoolnial Railway-to strengthen bridges, $385,000.
Mr. BARKER, We should have some explanation of this. Will this vote close the whole item for strengthening bridges, or is this to be continued from year to year?
This vote does not complete the transformation.

The total expenditure under this head from the commencement of the work in June. 1899. down to the 30th of June, 1903, was $867,101.04. and the expenditure from the 30th of June to the 1st |of May was $1G1.683.93. In addition to that, there is a superstructure for the southwest portion of the Miramichi bridge, $55,303.20; and a new- superstructure across the Restigouche river, $93,965.08. making a total to the 1st of May of $310,932.81, and a total expenditure of $1,178,084.45.

The total estimated cost of strengthening the bridges, exclusive of the Oxford and New Glasgow and Cape Breton Railway is $1,759,000. The larger class of engines are not in use on these railways at present, and it will not be immediately necessary to make the change in the bridges. '
Will the bon. gentleman now tell us how much of this appropriation of $385,000 there will be yet required to complete this expenditure of $1,759,000 ?
It is estimated that the amount required for 1904-5 will be $280,000.
There was an attempt made last year to find out where we were going to wind up with this expenditure for the strengthening of bridges. This is what was said :
Then there is the vote of $165,000 to be added to that, and the hon. gentleman says that will complete the repairs on those bridges.
I stated that this appropriation for the year will probably finish the work, but the general manager says it will take another year. There will he something further to be done.
You do not know what the amount is ?

I have not
the estimates at hand.
For the total repairs of bridges ?

For strength-[DOT]ening the bridges.
I think the committee last year understood that they were getting some idea from the Minister of Finance of where we were going to wind up in this expenditure on [DOT]capital account for strengthening bridges ; but I find that although that $165,000 has been spent, the hon. gentleman now asks us for $385,000 for this year and tells us that we shall have $280,000 afterwards. The Finance Minister may have had something lit his mind different from what we had, but certainly I think the House was led to believe that we were approaching the end of this expenditure. I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Railways if he will state the names of the particular bridges that are yet to be strengthened and the amount that will be required for each bridge. It is necessary to get that, I think, otherwise there will never apparently be an end to this.
To save time I will furnish my hon. friend with a statement of that.
My object is to get it on ' Hansard, ' if it is not too long, because that is the only way we can keep trace of it.

I will give a list of forty bridges for which the Dominion Bridge Company has a contract. I can give the names of the bridges, but not the exact amount required for each bridge. I could probably furnish that later.
The hon. minister will not expect us to pass the item until we get the fullest information.
The Finance Minister will see how necessary it is that we should have the figares.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is fair ; I do not object to that.

I could not give the cost with respect to each particular bridge *at this time, and it may be necessary to allow the item to stand, or, if my hon. friends will pass the item, I will furnish the particular information and place it on ' Hansard. '
The hon. minister is a little innocent. We have had promises of that kind before. I have no doubt he intends to fulfil his 'promise, and give a new example, but I do not think we can trust him.

We have discussed fhe strengthening of these bridges for two or -three years. Last year a certain bridge was said not to be worn out, but was transferred to the Prince Edward Island Railway. We were not able to ascertain last Mr. BARKER.
year what credit was given to the Intercolonial Railway for that bridge taken to the Prince Edward Island Railway or to get any information as to what wTas done when an old bridge was taken into stores and afterwards sold. The Finance Minister was quite certain that when it was taken into stores and sold that amount was credited to capital account, but lie was unable then (o give us his assurance that that had been done in any previous case although he was quite sure that it was going to be done in the particular case he was speaking of. But the time had net yet come for him to do it and he could not show the credit. Perhaps some of th se bridges were dealt with last year and the present minister will be able to tell the committee when it is up again exactly what was done with any bridges that were taken into stores last year or sent over to the Prince Edward Island Railway and placed there. Was the value of those bridges credited to capital account ? Although the Minister of Finance said that was the practice, to charge the new bridge to capital and to credit capital with the value of the old bridge, I do not wish to be understood as conceding for a moment that that is the proper way to deal with it. I think it is just as objectionable to deal with the bridges in that way as to deal with rails in the way this government 'has been dealing with them since 1896. It is cheating capital account for the benefit of revenue. What the Finance Minister thought was going to be done last year in some instances would have had the effect of increasing the revenue and adding to the capital debt of the road. Supposing an old bridge cost originally $100,000 and that the hon. gentleman, when renewing it, had to put up a better bridge in order to carry the heavier locomotives, erected a bridge costing $120,000 and sold the cld bridge for $50,000. Now as I understand, the hon. gentleman charges the $120,000 to capital and credits capital with $50,000 blit the hon. gentleman must see that if he were not 'increasing the weight of the bridge but simply substituting another $100,000 bridge he would have to charge the whole $100,000 to revenue and credit revenue with the $5,000 and. therefore, his revenue account would have lost $50,000 by the renewal of that bridge. By liis method he escapes such a charge altogether and this practice makes a difference of hundreds of thousands of dollars every year. In fact, he has kept his account with reference to steel rails and old bridges in such a way that it is absolutely impossible to find out the amount of the deficit of each year which should take the place of the small profits he has been claiming. There is no doubt that in the case I am speaking of. a betterment of $20,000, that amount should be dealt with as a betterment. the $20,000 being charged to capital account, and the remainder, or $100,000 dealt

With as a renewal of the old bridge, chargeable against revenue account, less the value of the old material or bridge taken out. The hon. gentleman did not seem last year to consider this worthy of his consideration.
To increase accommodation at Levis, $17,000.
. Mr. BMMEBSON. The amount asked -this year is $17,000 of which $12,000 is a revote. It is for completing i'he concrete platforms and1 curves and tank and some [DOT]electric wiring which with the engineering will bring the whole amount to $17,000.
Will that complete it ?
Yes.
What is the total expenditure on the station at Point Lfivis.

The total expenditure Tor increased accommodation for the commencement of the work June 30th, 1897, [DOT]down to the 1st of May, 1904, is $360,380.44, and Phe total estimated cost in connection with the increased accommodation at Levis was $393,000.
What was the total expenditure in that statement?
I have given the total, $360,380.44.
That is for increased accommodation ; I wanted to know the total expenditure at Point Levis.
It is impossible to give that because it was all voted in the sum for the purchase of the St. Charles brai cii and dees not appear in the accounts as the Levis terminals. [DOT]
It seems a very large sum. How much does the station, for example, cost ?

I cannot give the exact cost of the station ; it is not so much the expenditure on the station as in connection with the restricted area at Lfivis. As we all know the space between the bluff and the water's edge is very narrow and the arrangement of the tracks and t*he making :of the changes has been very expensive. The expenditure in connection with the station lias not been so very large although it is a very efficient and convenient station.
' Enormous ' is the proper word.
The area may be restricted but the expenditure certainly is not.
The more restricted the area, the more difficult it is to restrict the expenditure.
Coujd the minister not give us some idea as to the expenditure upon the building itself?

I could not give it tonight, but I will to-morrow.
Air-brakes to freight cars, $25,000.
How many freight cars will that furnish ?
500 cars at an average cost of $50 a car.
How many are equipped with air-brakes now?
Box cars, 5,279 ; all classes of cars, 9,782. Equipped with air brakes to 30th June, 1903, 0,030 ; total then to be equipped, 3,752. We estimate to be equipped during the year 1903-4, 500.
When new ears are bought are they equipped with the sijr brakes, or does the railway equip them afterwards ?
They are all equipped with air brakes.
How many more are there to be equipped ? (
As estimated, 3,752. We take about 500 each year.
How many were equipped last year ?
Five hundred.
According to ' Hansard ' of last year, at June 30th, 1903, you had 3,672 to be equipped. If you equipped 500 last year that would leave 3,172.
It was 3,752 at the 30th June, 1903.
According to ' Hansard ' it was 3.672.
Never mind.
This was the Finance Minister's statement, and surely we should take that. Did the minister buy any cars during 1904 ?
Yes.
How many freight cars ?
I am informed that there were 207 box cars, but I have not the figures as to the others, but I can get the information for the hon. gentleman.

I should be glad if the minister would furnish a statement showing how many new freight cars have been purchased with the brake equipment, and also how many cars out of service have been rebuilt and equipped. I want to see, in fact, how he used this $25,000 voted last year for this purpose. The same question would apply to the next item, that of draw-bars on freight cars ; and, perhaps, these two items had better stand until we get that information.
To exchange draw-bars of freight cars, $45,000.

The cost per car for the draw-bars is about $40. We are asking this year for $45,000 to provide draw-bars for 1,125 cars. The total expenditure for exchanging draw-bars from the commencement of the work to 30th June. 1903, is $105,000, and for the eleven months ending 31st May, 1904, $32,643.31.
What is a draw-bar?

It is the arrangement by which the cars are attached together- the coupler. There is a standard draw-bar used all over the continent. It is necessary to have your cars equipped with that standard draw-bar, in order that the cars may be transferred to other roads.
How many cars are furnished with the standard draw-bar, and how many are still to be equipped ?
The work has been going on for some time, and each year there is a vote to equip cars with the standard draw-bar.
It is important to know the number, in view of future expenditure.

Up to the 30th of June we have changed 6.876, we have a balance to change after June, 1903, of 2,906.< It was estimated that up to the 30th of June last there were to be changed 1,150. That work will probably have been completed. The estimate to be charged to June 30 this year, is 1,756, and we provide by this vote to change 1,125.
Who has the contract for these draw-bars ?
The draw-bars are furnished by tender and competition, and the work of changing is done in the shops at Moncton. We purchase the draw-bars and do the rest of the work in the shops.
Who is the successful tenderer ?
I could not tell that. Perhaps Mr. Pottinger would know.
Is the hon. gentleman quite sure they were purchased by tender ?
My deputy says so, and that has been the usual course since I came into the department.
Would the hon. gentleman add this to the list of items on which he is to furnish information, and ask the proper officer ?

In connection with this item, could the hon. gentleman inform us as to the amount we have paid for increased ter-Mr. BARKER.
minal facilities to the Grand Trunk Railway at Montreal ?
That is an annual sum, paid yearly.
It increases when the facilities are increased ?

I do not think any increased sum has been paid this year. No claims of that character have come under my observation yet. Replying to the leader of the opposition, I will give the name of the successful tenderer to-morrow.

I would also like the minister to be able to tell us to-morrow to what extent side ladders instead of end ladders have been put upon his freight cars; also, if it is to his knowledge that other railway companies in Canada are making a similar provision.

We want the item respecting draw-bars to stand, that we may ascertain who got the contract and when.
New machinery for locomotive and car shops, $31,000.
What is the total contemplated expenditure ?

The total estimated cost for new machinery for the locomotives in the car shops, to the 30th of June, 1905, is $181,247.33. The amount required to keep the shops up to date is estimated to be about $25,000 a year.
What is the total expenditure on toojs and machinery used in these shops ?

About $132,000. Since 1888 the total cost of machinery and tools, up to the 1st of May, 1904, has been $131,845.40. Machinery is being placed in ail the shops. In regard to new shops, we have to modernize the machinery and make the tools up to date. It is supposed that the expenditure will average about $25,000 each year for that purpose.
I think the minister must be mistaken. From 1888 to 1904 is sixteen years, and he said the total expenditure for machinery in the shops and the extension of the shops was only $131,000.
That does not include the shops themselves, only the tools and machinery.
I thought the expenditure was largely in excess of that.

It appears not.
Some resolutions reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will we take up to-morrow ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We will take up the Railway Bill followed by the motion for supply and my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals will resume his estimates.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.45 p.m.	[DOT]
Tuesday, July 5th, 1904.
